content.goal: Ask the model for JSON in the prompt (Level 1). Add a classify() function to atlas.py.
content.why: This is Level 1 from the theory — just ask. It often works, but it is fragile. You will feel that fragility, then fix it. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 5, section 5.3.)
content.code:
import json

def classify_level1(text):
    reply = ask([
        {"role": "system", "content":
         "Classify the bug report's severity as one of BLOCKER, MAJOR, MINOR, TRIVIAL. "
         "Reply with ONLY a JSON object: {\"severity\": \"...\", \"component\": \"...\"}"},
        {"role": "user", "content": text},
    ])
    return reply

print(classify_level1("Users cannot log in at all since this morning."))
content.verify: You get JSON-looking text back, likely {"severity": "BLOCKER", ...}. Note it is still a STRING, and the model may wrap it in prose or code fences on some runs.

content.goal: Force valid JSON at the provider level (Level 2). Update ask() to accept a json_mode flag.
content.why: Most OpenAI-compatible providers can GUARANTEE syntactically valid JSON, removing stray prose and broken syntax. This is Level 2. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 5, section 5.3.)
content.verify: The file saves. Calling ask(..., json_mode=True) will now return only valid JSON text — no prose, no fences.
content.troubleshoot: If your provider rejects response_format, it may not support JSON mode for that model. Fall back to a strong Level-1 prompt ("reply with ONLY JSON") and rely on the Level-3 validation in the next step to catch problems.

content.goal: Define the exact shape you expect and VALIDATE against it (Level 3). Install pydantic.
content.why: Level 2 guarantees valid JSON, not the RIGHT fields and types. A schema closes that gap — the professional default. Pydantic plays the role your Java validation annotations play. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 5, section 5.3.)
content.verify: pydantic installs without error. Run `pip list` and confirm it appears.

content.goal: Add a schema and a validating classify() to atlas.py.
content.why: Now the output is BOTH valid JSON AND the exact structure you require. Anything malformed is rejected, not silently trusted. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 5.)
content.verify: You get a validated Triage object, e.g. severity='BLOCKER' component='login'. If the model returned a bad severity, pydantic raises a clear ValidationError instead of letting garbage through.

content.goal: Add self-correction — feed a validation error back to the model and retry.
content.why: A fallible generator wrapped in a checking loop is the deepest recurring shape in agentic engineering. This previews reflection (Ch 7). (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 5, section 5.4.)
content.verify: classify_safe() returns a valid Triage even if the first attempt was malformed — you can see it recover by printing each attempt. On a well-behaved model it succeeds on the first try.

content.goal: CHECKPOINT — you can get data, not just prose, from the model.
content.why: Structured output is the bridge to tools. Confirm it works before Unit 4 gives the model a tool.
content.verify: All true — classify() returns a typed, validated object; bad output raises a clear error; classify_safe() recovers from a malformed first attempt. You now understand that tool use (next unit) is this same structured-output skill with a dedicated channel.
